notes.okukuba: Okukuba engoma: to play the drum.
notes.abayimba: Relative: abantu abayimba, the people who sing.

guidebook.intro: Ganda music is built on drums, xylophones and harps, and songs carry history, praise and humour. This unit also shows how to say “the one who…”.

tips.title: “Who” and “which”: add the vowel back
body: A verb that describes a noun (“the people who sing”) takes the noun’s initial vowel: **abantu bayimba** is “the people sing”, but **abantu abayimba** is “the people who sing”. **Ekintu kigwa** is “the thing falls”; **ekintu ekigwa** is “the thing that falls”.
For one person (**omu-** nouns) the written form is **a-** in both, and only the tone changes: **omusadha akuba engoma** can mean “the man plays the drum” or “the man who plays the drum”.

culture.title: The royal drums
body: Drums once carried messages between villages and announced the Kabaka. The royal drums, **Mujaguzo**, are beaten at coronations and great royal occasions, and a Kabaka was said to “eat Buganda” when he took the throne to their sound.

culture.title: Bakisimba
body: **Bakisimba** is the best-known Ganda dance, danced mostly with the waist to drums and amadinda. Its name comes from words said to be spoken when the first banana wine was made: “they planted the banana”.
